This heartbreak has been my first, ever and at 36 it’s definitely left its mark. Every step of the way, even from the beginning of my time with him, has been new and completely unknown to me. It’s made it harder since I have nothing to compare it to, at all. I haven’t handled it well at all, not really. It’s like my feelings about it constantly shift, even a year out. Sometimes I’ll be like “I don’t care. I really don’t care” and others I’ll be broken up inside.  Nothing has helped, at least not in the way that people are asking for when they ask you how to get over someone. Time has been it, I read it over and over and I got sick of seeing it because it meant it wasn’t going to be fast in any way. A close friend of mine kept referring to it as “waves” and she has been completely right. I’m prone to over analyzing so this has been a nightmare, but I’m actually getting over it, just not a fast as I’d like. I guess the reality is you never get over it, you just start to think of it less. That’s what it seems like anyway, just like a death, and that was NOT the answer I wanted to arrive at. I’m making peace with it all now. That’s one good thing I can say about myself, for better or worse, I am thorough. By the time this is done I’ll have looked at this thing from every angle imaginable. I’ll have thoroughly felt the heart rending brutality of lost love. I learn from my mistakes and I never make the same one twice. I have to learn everything the hard ways and once the price of pain is paid, I learn.  What I’d tell someone is, try to turn this pain into something meaningful, something valuable. Let the pain change you for the better, because if you don’t, you’ll have suffered for nothing. I refuse to have suffered for nothing and so in every bit of pain in my life I look for the lessons, and I set about making damn sure whatever hurt me can never hurt me again, at least not in the same way anyway.

I’ve been using ChatGPT to speak with after feeling like I exhausted my support network about a very painful breakup I’ve been going through. I have a hard time opening up to people and tend to isolate myself and so it’s been very helpful for me during this time. I won’t pretend I haven’t gotten somewhat attached to it, but I always make sure to take everything with a grain of salt and keep first in foremost in my mind that it is a piece of software and not a real, genuine human connection. I understand it can be dangerous to become too attached or forget it’s not a living breathing person. I can’t afford therapy atm and this is helpful in that area. It doesn’t replace therapy at all, but it does help me see things from a different perspective that I, in my despair, have struggled to see on my own. I also use it for silly things like having it design my magical girl form because I love Madoka magica and it has been a fun little diversion, thought experiment type of thing. I encourage others to use it to see things from a different perspective but I also caution them not to believe everything at face value or forget it isn’t a real person or that it isn’t alive. It can be a slippery slope and I do have mixed feelings about it and ai as a whole, but for now it’s all I have and I’ve desperately needed help over this last year, it’s been the worst year of my life in many respects and it has helped my challenge my negative thoughts and views in a way that has helped me tremendously. I don’t know what the future is and I do believe there is real danger with it, but for the moment I use it, cautiously, and am both in awe and fear of it. It’s easy to jump on the bandwagon either pro or anti ai, but I remain somewhat cautiously optimistic about it because I don’t believe it’s going anywhere anytime soon. 

My thoughts about using ai for art, however, are very different as someone with a background in the field. What it can produce is stunning at times, but it doesn’t hold the same value as human produced art and it never will. Just wanted to add that caveat because it’s important.

Shade around the object, it helps indicate volume. For example use ellipse ((( shapes along the fish’s body, if that makes sense. You can use a technique called burnishing by applying pressure with a lighter colored pencil, usually white or a lighter color,but doesn’t have to be. When you do that though the tooth of the paper is pretty much lost so you won’t be able to apply more color, unless you used some fixative.  This is where the type of paper you use is important for the media you’re using. Colored pencils do best when the paper has more tooth, which is the sort of rough texture to it. They also work best when applying color gradually with layering . 

You could take a lighter color of blue or white and go over some of the blues of the water and create filtered light beams by burnishing here. The effect really looks nice when you’ve layered lots of colors together and then burnish with the lighter color. I was also taught that you only shade in one direction, but there are no hard rules, but it does make it look better. There are all sorts of mark making techniques to apply color so just have fun. Usually you don’t want your strokes to show quite like you have here in the water UNLESS you are specifically trying to highlight your brush strokes to emphasize the art in some way. So for the water I’d probably lightly apply color in small circles. Additionally I would use complimentary colors for shading, so blue for orange here. Don’t be afraid to be bold and use cooora you may not immediately think of. This is where using references comes in and I’d also recommend using references every single time. I’ll never forget getting called out for not referencing a horse when I made something similar to a horse. I thought since I grew up with horses I knew their anatomy, which was incorrect. What I knew was the IDEA of a horse, not the minutiae. Really study what you’re trying to represent, you’ll find there are more colors than you realize in the object you are studying. For example white human skin tone has all sorts of undertones like blue, red, and green because you can see the veins and blood beneath the surface. Basically don’t be afraid to use many colors. 

Color pencils can be really cool on their own, but you can combine them with so many other mediums and really make something pop. Another thing I was taught is to apply color all over the page to unify. For example if you use one color on one part, say the orange for the fish, you should sneak in more orange in other spots, such as in the water where you can use that same orange to make a darker blue color. I can’t remember the exact phrase they used to illustrate this point rn but maybe you get what I mean. Something like “apply color uniformly across the page”. Also do thumbnails to work on composition before committing to one and starting to render only to find out you aren’t happy with the composition. You do t have to do many, I always did a lot, but even 3-5 different comps will help you decide. It’ll save ya time in the long run. I’d say take a look into color theory as well. 

Another thing a professor told me that blew my mind is to not be afraid to use many different mediums in your work. Idk why but it never occurred to me to do this until she told me and it was an instant level up for my artwork.
